headline: A placebo sold as caffeine improved sport performance by a small-to-moderate amount in 17 low-quality studies
question: How much does a placebo, described to people as caffeine, change sport performance?
design: A systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of studies in healthy adults, searched from database start to July 2026 (English, peer-reviewed only). Seventeen studies were included, with 257 participants in all (median age 23 years; 82% men; 12 studies men only, one women only). Twelve studies used trained and five untrained people. Nine studies measured weightlifting, five running and three cycling. In each study, people were told a placebo was caffeine and their performance was compared with a baseline or no-treatment condition. Five studies also gave real caffeine, but the pooled analysis compares only placebo with baseline or no treatment. The authors rated risk of bias with the Cochrane tool and certainty with GRADE. The protocol was registered (OSF).
findings:
Pooled effect of placebo caffeine on performance: standardised mean difference d = 0.49 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.69), a small-to-moderate benefit; the prediction interval was 0.01 to 0.96. Heterogeneity was low (I² = 21%), and removing any one study left d between 0.43 and 0.53.

In meta-regression, the effect was larger when researchers were blinded to the treatment (b = 0.52, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.99) and smaller as the share of women in a sample rose (b = −0.93, 95% CI −1.68 to −0.19). No other factor tested, such as sport, training status or timing, changed it.

Among secondary outcomes, perceived exertion (RPE) also favoured the placebo (d = 0.52, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.78; 11 studies), and more steps to build the expectation gave a larger RPE effect (b = 0.21, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.41).

GRADE certainty was low for the main result and low to very low across all analyses.
limits: All 17 studies were at risk of bias: nine high and eight unclear. Allocation concealment was at high risk in over half (9 studies), blinding of participants or researchers was missing in nearly half (8), and whether people believed the placebo (a manipulation check) was unclear in three-quarters (13). The total of 257 people is small, and 82% were men, so the result may not hold for women. The comparison is placebo against no treatment, which also picks up the effect of simply being tested. The prediction interval reaches 0.01, so a new study could find almost no effect. Six studies gave the placebo less than 20 min before the task, which may have made people doubt it. Studies differ in task (lifting, running, cycling), so one pooled number mixes very different outcomes. Only English, peer-reviewed papers were searched. The review had no funding and the authors declare no conflicts. The authors themselves call the evidence low quality and ask for better designs.
meaning: The caffeine lesson (sup-caffeine) teaches that real caffeine gives about 2% faster time trials. This review shows that belief alone may give part of such a gain, so a trial of caffeine needs a placebo group that cannot tell which pill it got. It does not say caffeine is a placebo: the pooled studies compared deception with no treatment, not real caffeine with placebo. It is also a lesson in appraisal (ev-pyramid): a pooled result from weak, biased studies stays weak. The sup-caffeine lesson stands.

variants.stem: A review finds that a placebo sold as caffeine gives d = 0.49 for performance. What does that show?

options.text: Expecting caffeine alone may improve performance, apart from the drug
options.why: Right: the studies compared deceptive placebo with no treatment, so the gain comes from expectation.

options.text: Real caffeine works only through expectation
options.why: The pooled analysis compared placebo with no treatment, not real caffeine with placebo, so it says nothing about the drug's own effect.

options.text: An honestly labelled placebo works just as well
options.why: No study gave an honestly labelled placebo; all of them used deception.
No doses were tested: the people got an inert pill.

variants.stem: What most limits how far to trust the pooled placebo-caffeine effect?

options.text: All 17 studies were at high or unclear risk of bias and total n was only 257
options.why: Right: GRADE certainty was low to very low, with poor allocation concealment and manipulation checks unclear in most studies.

options.text: A coffee company paid for the review
options.why: The authors report no funding and no conflicts of interest.

options.text: The review pooled studies in rats and humans
options.why: It included healthy human adults only.

options.text: Heterogeneity between studies was very high (I² above 90%)
options.why: The authors report low heterogeneity; the problem is study quality.

variants.stem: In the 2026 placebo-caffeine review, effects were larger in studies where researchers did not know the pill was a placebo. What is the careful reading?

options.text: Researchers who know may dampen belief; a lead to test, not proof
options.why: Right: the authors suggest a researcher who knows it is a placebo may change instructions or manner without meaning to. It is one study-level meta-regression, b = 0.52 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.99), so it is a lead, not proof.

options.text: Blinding researchers is useless in supplement trials
options.why: Blinding guards against exactly this kind of bias; the result is a reason to keep it.

options.text: Blinding researchers makes any placebo work better for everyone
options.why: That is a causal claim about every person from one study-level meta-regression with a wide interval.

options.text: Unblinded studies should be dropped since they show no effect
options.why: Unblinded studies still showed effects; the regression shows a difference in size, with a wide interval (0.01 to 0.99).
